topic: What happens if you spin in a chair?
title: What spinning in a chair does
hook: What happens if you spin in a chair?

beats.line: Each inner ear has three fluid-filled loops that sense every turn.
Start spinning, and that fluid swirls, telling your brain you're turning.
Spin at a steady speed, and within about twenty seconds you barely feel it.
Then stop, and the fluid keeps swirling, so the room seems to spin.
Ballet dancers train their brains to feel far less of this dizziness.

end.line: How many spins before you get dizzy?

description: Why the room keeps turning after you stop spinning, and how ballet dancers train their brains to beat dizziness.

facts.claim: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals: fluid-filled loops set roughly at right angles that tell the brain when the head rotates.
When you start turning, the fluid lags behind the canal walls and bends the cupula over hair cells, which signal the rotation to the brain.
facts.source: NIDCD / Biology LibreTexts, Human Physiology 10.5 (Vestibular system)

facts.claim: During steady rotation the fluid catches up with the canal, so the sensation of turning fades within roughly 15-20 seconds.
facts.source: Biology LibreTexts, Human Physiology 10.5 / Purves, Neuroscience (vestibular system)

facts.claim: When the rotation stops, the fluid keeps moving briefly and bends the cupula the other way, so the surroundings seem to keep spinning.
facts.source: Biology LibreTexts, Human Physiology 10.5 / Purves, Neuroscience

facts.claim: Imperial College study (29 ballet dancers vs 20 rowers): after being spun in a chair, dancers felt less dizzy, with training-related brain differences in the cerebellum and cortex.
facts.source: Nigmatullina et al., Cerebral Cortex 2013 (PubMed 24072889) / Imperial College London news
